```
The world’s giraffe population is roughly 120,000 animals (about 117,000 in the wild across the four species—Southern ~55k, Masai ~45k, Reticulated ~16k, Northern ~6k—plus ~2,000 in captivity). Their coat patterns differ by species: large polygonal blotches (Reticulated, ~400 spots each), round blotches (Southern, ~350 each), large rectangular patches (Northern, ~250 each), and numerous small jagged “vine-leaf” spots (Masai, ~1,100 each). Weighting by population gives an average of about 630 spots per giraffe over ~12 m² of spotted skin. Multiplying:

120,000 giraffes × ~625 spots ≈ 75,000,000

75,000,000
```

There are roughly 110,000–120,000 giraffes alive today (about 110,000 in the wild across the four species—Southern ~55k, Masai ~35k–45k, Reticulated ~16k, Northern ~6k—plus ~1,500 in captivity).

Spot counts differ by species:
- Northern: large rectangular patches (~150–180 each)
- Reticulated: large polygonal patches (~200–250 each)
- Southern: round/blotched spots (~300–350 each)
- Masai: smaller, darker, irregular spots (~400–500 each)

That gives a population-weighted average of about 300–320 distinct spots per giraffe.

Multiplying:
~115,000 giraffes × ~310 spots ≈ 35.7 million

So my single best point estimate is:

36,000,000
```

There are roughly 115,000 giraffes alive today (about 110,000–117,000 in the wild across Africa plus ~1,500–2,000 in captivity). Breaking them into the four species/subspecies by typical coat pattern density:

- Reticulated (~16,000 individuals): large polygonal spots → ~250 spots each

- Southern (~55,000): round, medium-sized spots → ~350 spots each  
- Northern (~6,000): large rectangular patches → ~180 spots each  

That gives a population-weighted average of about 320 dark spots per giraffe. Multiplying:

115,000 × 320 ≈ 36,800,000

Rounding to a single point estimate:

35,000,000

There are roughly 117,000 wild giraffes (all four species/subspecies combined, with Southern and Masai making up the bulk) plus about 1,500–2,000 in captivity, so ~119,000 living giraffes total.

Spot density varies by species:
- Masai (≈35,000): small, irregular, dense spots → ~450 each
- Southern (≈55,000): round/blotched, medium density → ~250 each
- Reticulated (≈16,000): large polygonal patches with thin lines → ~150 each
- Northern (≈6,000): large rectangular blocks → ~180 each
- Captive (≈2,000): mixed, averaging ~300 each

Body area carrying spots (neck, torso, upper legs, tail) is about 7–8 m² per animal. Weighting the populations gives an average of roughly 300 dark spots per giraffe.

119,000 × ~300 ≈ 35,700,000.

35,000,000

There are roughly 117,000 wild giraffes (plus ~1,800 in captivity), split mainly among four species with very different spot patterns:

- **Reticulated** (~16,000): large polygonal blocks → ~200 spots each  
- **Masai** (~45,000): small, dense, irregular blotches → ~500 spots each  
- **Southern** (~48,000): round/oval spots of moderate size → ~350 spots each  
- **Northern** (~6,000): large rectangular patches → ~150 spots each  

Weighted average ≈ 385 spots per giraffe.  
Total giraffes ≈ 119,000.

119,000 × 385 ≈ 45.8 million. Calibrating slightly downward for unspotted belly/inner-leg areas and juvenile sizes, the best point estimate is:

45000000
```

Quick reasoning: There are roughly 117,000 giraffes alive today (wild + captive), spread across four species with different spot patterns. Weighting by population:
- Southern giraffe (~55,000): medium blotches, ~350–400 spots each

- Northern giraffe (~6,000): large rectangular blotches plus leg spots, ~200–250 each

So I estimate **45,000,000** black/dark spots across all living giraffes — which is above your 40,000,000 threshold.
